utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, the accused are present. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic for the Beara Defence team, Ms. Nikolic, Mr. Josse, and that's about it. Witness is already present in the courtroom. Good morning, Doctor. How are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest after yesterday's ordeal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. We can therefore proceed. Hopefully we should finish with your testimony today. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Kwon is reminding me we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge Stole will be with us later on. At the moment, he is occupied with other official business of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, before I begin, if I may just introduce my colleague from the United States, Leah Erickson who's assisting us here, and she was here as well yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She was trying to point find out how to enter into the courtroom, and we helped her.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are most welcome, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Ostojic [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a couple of hours or so left. I'm going to try to shorten it, and thank you for your patience in that regard. Yesterday, we left off discussing matching rates and collection rates, and I want to know from you if you can share with us what constitutes a match according to the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's actually a slightly different issue than a matching rate, and this goes to how a positive or personal identification is established. A match, the term "match" in the notion of comparison, suggests that there are two separate objects, one being known and one being unknown, and that you are comparing class characteristics to establish whether the two are identical. So in a case involving DNA such as is typically referred to as a match, there would be a biological sample left at a scene, there would be a known sample taken from an accused, and the two would be compared to each other to a degree of scientific certainty. What ICMP is referring to when it does its DNA identifications is actually a statement of statistical probability, so ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and I don't mean to -- just so that we can follow along with you, and the ICMP actually does have that match definition or -- under their standard operating procedures, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of SOPs or protocols that deal with how exactly they go about establishing it. It's a multistep process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you don't mind, if we can just turn our attention to Exhibit P3224, which is the SOP statistical calculation of DNA-based identifications, and specifically once we see that document P3224, if we could turn to page 06248601. And I apologize that -- but I just wanted us to be able to follow along with you. As you were saying, using that nomenclature listed on that page, how does the ICMP create a match between a DNA sample and an individual?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be -- there are two profiles generated. One is of the known provided by the family member who -- or family members who are serving as the reference sample, so that is your known. They are comparing those against the samples or profiles being created from the bones and/or human remains that are being exhumed and analysed, but it isn't the same sort of match as a comparison of the two. Essentially, what happens is that the ICMP is using a series of family members of varying degrees of relatedness as their known, and it produces a statistical statement as to the probability that the unknown, the bone sample profile, whether it is related in some form to the individuals that are providing the reference sample.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, how many people would they need in order to create a match as even defined by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an ideal situation, what we are talking about is autosomal DNA, so it's your nuclear DNA that recombines -- it's a combination of each of your parents. It recombines and it forms your unique profile. In an ideal world, that forms a triangle, and you need all three pieces of the triangle to make the identification. Because given the high death rate that occurs in this circumstance, they are obligated to go outside of that triangle and use relationships and relatives in addition or to supplement those that are available. According to the protocol, essentially what they are looking for is three relatives to form the basis for the identification or to provide a sample against which bone samples are compared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you've just said in your previous answer on page 3, lines 13 through 14, you say that they are comparing those against the samples of other profiles -- I'm sorry. It was line 16 and 17. You say, "family members of varying degrees of relatedness as they are known, and it produces a statistical statement." When we say "relatedness," what does ICMP to the best of your experience and knowledge, what individuals do they use if they utilize those three? Can you give us a description -- is it a spouse? You've identified "other." I would imagine spouse is one.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- well, spouse has no biological relationship to the individual, although they are included on the list of potential donors that ICMP uses as their protocol. When a spouse would play into the equation is if what must be also present is a biological child of those two, so you would have the decedent who is the unknown, you would have the spouse who is known, but to use the spouse you would have to have a child known to be a biological product of the spouse and the decedent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak of relatedness, are you speaking in terms of, like, a half-sibling or a sibling?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. If you look at the Exhibit page 14 of 16 in the SOP that you called our attention to, it gives the list of what ICMP identified as potential donors. Many of those include others, some include half-siblings, they do include spouses, and so on. So cousins, grandparents, anybody with a biological blood relationship to the missing in addition to spouses can contribute and be used in the equation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you formulated an opinion as to whether or not within acceptable anthropological certainty to use a spouse, a half-sibling and let's say a cousin, for example, in order to generate a positive match?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the closer you are to a triangle, the parents and the sibling is your best statement of probability. The farther or the more distant the relationship, obviously because you are talking about complete recombination with each generation, you lose the specificity that is involved for this particular event. So obviously, a parent or two sets of parents would be infinitely preferable to grandparents or cousins or half-siblings or a spouse, which absent a child has absolutely no relationship and shouldn't be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, from your review of the SOPs of ICMP, have you seen whether or not they require or mandate that if they are using a spouse as one of the three for purposes of identification, that they also -- or were required or mandated to use an individual such as the child's couple? Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that stated in the SOP, but I -- you know, just because something isn't written down doesn't inherently make it not practice. I would -- there would be no relationship absent that, and I can't imagine anybody that knows even fundamentals about DNA would allow that to occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just going back briefly to some articles, and I know that you've spent sometime working with ICMP and you are familiar, obviously, with their protocols having reviewed them and their SOPs here. There is, as you would know, in your academic world other employees or former employees of ICMP who have written quite extensively about their experience with ICMP. Are you familiar with those articles?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of three of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is one of them -- just if we can go through it, if I can show it to you, 2D538. And I think just for the record, I think you identified that in Section 1.4 of your report. And if I may just continue while we are getting this up on the screen, now, some of these articles, although we are looking at one specifically, 2D538, it really seems from my review of that after having read it from the citation in your report; or tell us, what's the view of the former employees in general, if you can share that, from ICMP in connection with the practices within ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most consistent message in all of three of those is that DNA alone cannot and should not be used as the sole basis for an identification, and all three make note of the fact that it is the obligation of the forensic community to dispel the widely held miss conception that DNA forms a basis of an identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what other than DNA should be utilized, in your opinion, in connection with that for purposes of identification?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To scientifically establish identity beyond a reasonable doubt or to a degree of medical certainty, there has to be what is called individualisation or a unique identifier. There has to be something which distinguishes that individual beyond exclusion and beyond the inclusion of others, so it can't simply be everything matches, nothing doesn't. There has to be compelling evidence that the identity has been established absent any other possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, would I be correct, and -- does that include also the anthropological process, reliance on that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another portion of it. Essentially, what several of these articles describe and the third in particular are specific cases in which the DNA said there was a match, but even cursory examination of the remains showed that either multiple individuals were present or that the element that was being sampled and provided the DNA sample was not consistent, and ultimately, further DNA test proved that it did not match the rest of the remains. So essentially, because of the way the exhumation process happened, you do have co-mingling there's multiple individuals represented in bags, and that's understood. When it comes to the repatriation process, identifying the people and giving them back to their families, there is obviously a professional moral obligation to ensure that what you are returning represents solely the individual that has been identified and is purported to be, and what these particular papers and specifically the third paper reference is very specific examples within the ICMP of when that does not occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Doctor, let's briefly look at this third article by -- I think it's Professor Yazedjian, which is 2D540. Again, just 2D540. And there, I believe, they discuss the -- as the title I think indicates the importance of using traditional anthropological methods in DNA-led identification system, and in fact, I think if you read, as I'm sure you have, the article, they cite four specific examples which they categorized as mistakes that occurred by reliance on solely DNA. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They highlight four particular examples that they use as illustrative purposes that reliance solely on DNA leads to problems, and in fact, they have identified cases where significant problems would have occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's that position from the former employees of ICMP that there seems to be some urgency or at least some -- a request that ICMP start to rely on more of the anthropological process as we've discussed in addition to what you stated just moments ago?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overall purpose of the paper is that the focus of this -- and these essentially represent abstracts of papers that were presented at professional conferences, specifically the American Academy of Forensic Sciences, that was it a express and a plea over three years from the employees of the ICMP that -- to dispel the notion both in the community, in lay people and within the ICMP that DNA alone is answering this question, that there has to be additional review of the remains; there has to be the anthropological and pathological component to the identification process, not solely to the analysis for purposes of determining cause of death, but that it must continue through the identification phase so that we begin to deal with this issue of co-mingling and resolve multiple individuals who have essentially been lumped in falsely or inaccurately into representing one individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know in this article by Professor Yazedjian, they discuss the mistake of identification with a partial body and then the aging process -- not the aging process but the age estimate being 45 to 55, and then upon further review it was noted that it was 23-year-old after examining the femur. What my question to you in connection with that is, and we've had an opportunity to review the article, is why are these mistakes in identification significant when -- in calculating MNI?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem that begins in the field, goes through the analysis, and ultimately is revealed in the identification phase is that when co-mingling is present and re-association is not consistently attempted and acknowledged, that what you have is a system that samples DNA from selected elements only. What these cases and these articles highlight is that because we know there is co-mingling, if all you do is sample the arm and the leg, all the DNA profile shows is that that arm and that leg belongs to whoever it is ultimately identified to. The remainder of the elements, the skeletal elements contained in the bag or with the individual have not yet been established as belonging to that person because we are not talking about a fleshed body. We are talking about a collection of elements that even by Richard Wright and others who are in the field are admitted that, you know, this is a collection of people and we will continue the process of dividing them further down the line, unless that occurs, then what you hand back to families is a collection of bones in a bag of which all that can be established is whatever bone the DNA is cut from is the only bone that can be conclusively shown to belong to that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can -- thank you. If we can move on to another topic which is, I think, highlighted somewhat in your report under paragraph 1.2. My question in relating to that, although it seems plain but I need it for the record, have you had it the opportunity to analyse and review the Excel database entitled "ICMP Data on the Identified Persons and DNA Matches Related to Srebrenica 1995"?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the material, if you could -- to the best of your recollection, that Dean Manning is relying upon in his latest report, which is, I think, 30th of November, 2007? Is that that raw data that we were referring to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's some lack of clarity. Some of it might be my fault; some of it might be in other places, but if I can take one minute of the Court's time to clarify something. The first Manning report occurs in June 2007 in which he begins to cite as his source of MNI ICMP reports. I have not seen nor has it been provided what the source of that data is. The first and only report that is issued from ICMP occurs in 2006, and it is a methodology report only. There is no statement of number within that report. The only databases, raw information, or other source of numbers doesn't occur until October 8th of 2007, several months after Dean Manning's first report. So the information that Manning is relying on in that first June 2007 report isn't from ICMP to the extent that we have -- that I have seen that information. I don't know where he is getting that from. It has not been made available for us to review. It would appear that he is introducing scientific evidence absent a scientific report he is citing. When the databases are available as of October 8th, 2007, it does appear, and in addition to the Parsons memo from November 2007, it does appear that Manning's second report in November does include some of that data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Can we now discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. President, there is no report that Mr. Manning refers to in the 2007 June summary. He refers to ICMP records, and in particular, as I stated yesterday, it is in the transcript that what he refers to is the raw data, and I think that is sufficiently clear. I know my colleague is well aware of that, so it's not a question of some report that exists independently of anything that's described in Mr. Manning's work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think -- Dr. Komar I think clarified that on her own, but I think after yesterday's discussion we agreed that he did not have a report, formal or otherwise, that he examined. We're just not sure if a report existed, and I believe the doctor is suggesting that it seems from his analysis and summary that he is relying on a report that we've never been in the possession of. We are not saying there is a report. We believe that there was not one because I'm sure they would have produced it. We think it might be some of the raw data, and I think Dr. Komar, and I'll allow her to answer that with your permission, she believes that he was seemingly suggestively relying on a report that we've never seen, so she was, I think, clarifying the record on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can, I'm not suggesting there is a report. He is relying on a source of data that we cannot analyse. He is introducing, and by the testimony that the Prosecution read yesterday, he's analysed some source of data himself, come to a conclusion, and written it into his report. This is the first introduction in any source I've seen of the use of DNA as establishing the MNI absent a scientific source from which it is coming. If there is a database, raw or otherwise, from ICMP in June of 2007 that he is using, it has not been made available to anybody else for review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll repeat to some extent what I said, but I will add that in the record as I mentioned, at page 19.003, there is a very clear reference as to what Mr. Manning was relying on. Specifically, it is referred to as Exhibit 3002. That is a page that is derived from a CD that is denominated under ERN D0002146. That is the information that was provided to the Defence, and that is the information that is provided to this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can actually deal with this on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Ostojic. I don't think you need to dwell on this any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I think the Doctor was just clarifying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, we were going to move on to the raw data, and just so the Court knows, this is evidence that is under seal, so it should not be broadcast to the public. And specifically, if we can first examine P3002. And then, Doctor, just for the record, if you could help us identify that so we know that we have the proper document before us, and it's quite a large document, I believe. It may take awhile. As the document is coming up, I think -- I know we don't. As the document -- if I may just continue to ask, and then I'm sure we'll be able to catch up in the interest of time. Thank you. Dr. Komar, you've had an opportunity to review the ICMP raw database as we've identified it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've identified one that to my records is from October of 2007.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that, did you analyse it as well?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us if you yourself did anything to -- and I don't want to use the word "reconfigure," but to examine it as you are analyzing it and reviewing it. Did you reconstruct it in any fashion internally for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With any Excel spreadsheet, you can query it. It doesn't alter the information. It simply re-orders the appearance in which it is presented to you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do such a process in reviewing this material?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And your specific re-organisation using the commands that you placed in without obviously changing the data, you developed and provided us with a copy of the report for us to be able to understand your explanation of the analysis that you had based upon the ICMP raw database, and that's reflected, I believe, in our Exhibit 2D543. I know you don't have the number, but you've provided us with the spreadsheet, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what we've referred to as the redacted spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to it as the redacted. It would just be the -- it would just be the one that you kind of reconfigured or readjusted for purposes of your analysis.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have an original here of Dr. Komar's and because -- I misspoke. I have the raw data from ICMP here, and I think Dr. Komar has her report after looking at this where she reconfigured it in order to be able to analyse it with more clarity. If the Court would like, I can have this tendered to the Prosecution so that he can examine it, and this, also, is under seal under P3002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Doctor, just so that I'm clear, the data that I have here in front of me, which we've identified with this court number P3002, this is a raw data, and just explain the process or methodology that you utilised once you received this data so that we can have a better understanding of it. I'll just show it to my learned friend, please.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Excel spreadsheet, there's a series of columns that represent different variabilities or pieces of information. In Column A, it's known as MP or the missing person, and it's a list of the surname and given name along with the father's name of the individuals who are missing and purported to be ultimately identified. By -- the simple query I did was to -- there's a tool search within the Excel programme that allows you to sort data by a series of parameters, and I simply have isolated a number of individuals that fall into a specific class together for the purposes of illustration counting an analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- the process -- the first step that you took, did you delete any duplicated matches of the same individual represented by multiple samples?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a process of deleting them so much as hiding them from view. You can simply take them out of the visual representation of the view. So the information is not lost. It's simply resorted in another manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a putative match?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A putative match is the first step in the identification process. Essentially, what you have -- it could also be known as a tentative match. You have either circumstantial evidence, witness statement, or some other source that suggests that a specific unidentified body might potentially be represented by a missing person; and therefore, you go through the process of confirming or scientifically verifying whether that person is or is not represented by those remains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you under your review and analysis accomplish that task?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't do that in this forum. Essentially what that database represents is the end result of that process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you find once you do your reconfiguration of this document in order to better analyse it for clarity?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is contained in this list of individuals a number -- large number of individuals for which the putative match or the missing person contains, not one, but between two and four individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me, what's the significance of that so that we can better understand that.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if we go to this idea of the DNA profile, what you have is a profile that is then compared to the very large database that contains all of the information from the references, the family members who have given their DNA as reference samples. There's a process by which the 15 alleles or gene parts that represent the part of the entire DNA structure they're looking at. It's compared to those individuals. When matches around found -- not matches. When similarities are found, you then go through progressive steps to determine whether or not there -- a statistical probability that that profile from the unknown bone is in fact related to a degree of statistical probability to the reference samples given by the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are they able to -- utilizing these two to four putative matches or individuals, are they able to determine or differentiate between one individual or another?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this database suggests and what the information contains, if I can show it to the Court - I don't know if I can; it's on my computer - what is listed under the missing person, so the identified individual is in fact not one person but a series of either two or four people. So essentially and where this becomes relevant to this statement of MNI, included in the statement of MNI as produced in both of Manning's reports and discussed somewhat in Parsons' memo, they argue for the inclusion of what is known as unique DNA profiles. And what they are arguing with that is that they have a series of profiles, DNA fingerprints, if you will, taken from bones that cannot and have not been associated with specific individuals. They argue that because these unique profiles exist but yet have not been matched, that number, which at the second report I believe is the 758 individuals, should be included in the ultimate collection or calculation of the MNI raising the number by 758 of the total number of people associated with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why this information is relevant is if you look at their own database and their own results, you have a very, high in the hundreds, number of individuals for which DNA profiles have been extracted from bone, and by their own calculation, that DNA profile, supposedly unique, matches between two and four people. So it's impossible to argue that something is unique if, in fact, it matches four people. Now, the 758 number they are arguing doesn't include those individuals, and let me be clear about that. What those individuals raise is the -- is evidence of the fact that what they call DNA profiles as being unique can't be unique. If it matches four, two, three, four people, that isn't a unique profile. And so the argument for including 758 of those profiles unassociated with actual identifications or named decedents is not a valid argument. It's not a valid conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Doctor, we do have now on e-court, I believe, the data that you reconfigured under number 2D543. So if we can just back up a little bit and, thank you, and we're getting to some of the final analysis in connection with the 500 and -- what are 758 purported unique DNA samples, but I'd like to just stick for a moment, and if you could just tell us as we have the one page on the document how you did it and you did it with respect to the putative matches, and if you could tell me whether the database includes the putative matches for individuals which were positively identified, and if you can tell me the number, and I think we've discussed it, so we should have it readily available. Or I could help you --

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not clear what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next -- the database includes a total of 473 putative matches for which individuals are listed as positively identified. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absent a specific report that details how ICMP is interpreting the database, all we can do is examine the raw database as I assume Mr. Manning did as well. The missing people and the title of the database is that these are individuals who have been identified and matches have been made. So one -- it's an assumption, I don't know if it's a safe assumption, is the argument, and given that there are case numbers, ICMP numbers, protocol numbers, et cetera, it suggests that these people have gone through the process and have been identified and that this is what they are -- these are the individuals they are including in that list of identified people. Included in that list are these individuals for which there are multiple people recognised as the identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is this group of 473 putative matches, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so I understand. So to distinguish it from what you were discussing earlier as reflected in Dean Manning's report of the 758?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding that those people are separate, and in fact, there is a separate ICMP database that includes 816 "unique biological profiles." So I'm not quite sure where the 753 number comes from if Mr. Manning is using the same in the November report, the same raw source of data. Essentially, ICMP is saying there's 816 of them. I don't know under what process or by what set of criteria a number of those would be removed to get to the 753 number, but essentially that's what we are talking about. The 400 people included in this list is in no way relevant to those 8 -- to that number of unique unidentified people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so I'm clear, Doctor, do you have an opinion based on a reasonable degree of scientific certainty as to whether or not it's acceptable for the ICMP to consider a putative match of two to four individuals as a "positive identification." ?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not be standard or acceptable practice. I guess the question I would like answered is, what is the next step that ICMP takes to attempt to resolve this? So to be completely fair to ICMP at this point, absent a report that expressly states how they would go about interpreting this raw data, what could be done to resolve these identifications? If you actually look at the identifications, and I apologise to the Court; I hope you can see this at some point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can - and I don't mean to interrupt - just kindly direct us to the page that you'd like us to look at. We have it in front of us on the e-court system -- we don't?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't a page. It's a database. You have to be able to scroll through it. I've got it up on my computer if we can switch -- if we can switch to your system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can do it. Apparently we're interconnected.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I do it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can Madam Usher please help.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I just think it's important to just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Of course, Mr. Ostojic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking at it, and I can't see it, so -- it's right -- it's right --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have it in front of us, Doctor, so --

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it. I can't see what you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me. Okay. There we go. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could just, then, lead us through so we could have a better appreciate appreciation for what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look -- it's this Column A marked missing person or the identified person, so you can see a list. It begins with surname. The father's name is parenthesized, and then the individual's given name occurs in the first list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or column?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First column. The first 16 are locked or frozen within the programme. That's simply an artifact of the programme, but if you look at the lower section where my cursor is, we are into the 5.000 numbers, 50.56, 5.057. If you look at the missing persons' names, you can see that in fact the surname is there, the father's name is there, but you have multiple first names or multiple individuals that are listed as "identified individuals." So they are essentially saying that the DNA profile extracted from a series of bones match to the same degree of statistical probability and statistical significance one, two, three, four people. And that's what I'm attempting to show with this particular database sorted as it is, that rather than filter these throughout as you look at 7.000 individuals until your eyes cross, if you separate them out you can see that there are hundreds of individuals or hundreds of "identifications" that in fact have only been reduced to family groups, so two, three, four related individuals. And that's not a positive identification in any sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we were to just take these 473 multiple identification matches, could we and have you analysed to determine whether they represent a minimum number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible to do that. Essentially what you have is a DNA profile that matches multiple individuals. So the profile is representing a bone. It's that the profile then matches not one person, but two, three, or four people. So it doesn't effect MNI in terms of that. How this relates to MNI is it illustrates an argument against simply relying on the presence of a DNA profile alone, absent any kind of conclusionary identification at somehow being admissible as evidence of an MNI or as a number of individuals to count unidentified DNA profiles as evidence of people, missing people, to elevate the MNI number is not appropriate since it shows that in fact no DNA sample -- or no DNA profile at the level they're looking at it is in fact unique.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would it be -- and it was -- you stated that it was unacceptable, but is it also in your opinion that it's misleading?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's unclear what my colleague's referring to as to what's misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic. I think you need to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, it's -- at least from a layperson when you look at it, and I think we've discussed it, and I want your opinion as to whether or not it's misleading for the ICMP to consider a putative match of two to four individuals as a positive identification. I know you said that it was unacceptable. Now I'm just asking you if it is misleading or not.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't state that ICMP is representing these as individuals. What the -- where there is a problem is that the interpretation of these numbers, the presentation of these numbers, is in fact not being done by ICMP; it's being done by Dean Manning. And so if he counts these individuals, it is possible that someone who is not familiar enough with DNA technology and how identifications are done that they would simply include all of these individuals in a calculation of MNI, whereas someone with sufficient knowledge as to how identifications are done would recognise that these people should not be included as yet being definitively and positively identified. So because the presentation of the number of MNI based solely on DNA data is in fact coming from Dean Manning and not ICMP with the absent of that Parsons memo which states a different number, I'm not saying the ICMP is saying these are identified people. The title of the database suggests that they are, but I would open that up to ICMP to confirm that that's in fact what they're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we are talking about a Dean Manning a little bit. Let's just look at his 27th of October, 2007, report which is in evidence as P2993, I believe, and if I can direct your attention to page number 06148657. And I think this is where you started discussing the 758 unique DNA samples that are not matched that you were referring to moments earlier in your testimony, and just correct me if I'm wrong on that or verify that I was correct.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're getting it.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, it's 06148657 is the ERN number. Would you like it --

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. There it is. So if you can look in the second section below the highlighted thing that says -- below the highlighted title that says "All Srebrenica Victims Identified Via DNA Analysis By ICMP," and there's a total number of 5.021. In the second paragraph -- or, sorry, in the third line of that paragraph, "In addition, ICMP records indicate that there are 758 unique Srebrenica-related DNA records which have not yet been matched to a missing person but that he includes in his calculation of MNI."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He being Dean Manning, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dean Manning. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. That's okay. What's the significance of that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including profile alone absent an identification is not scientifically sound. It's included as -- that there are profiles removed from the DNA or removed from bone elements is not being contested that they've done this, but by ICMP's own admission, they haven't matched them to any particular individual. The problem with including them based solely on profile is that, again, this notion of uniqueness is not correct. A statement of statistical probability that such as they are calculating from ICMP is solely reliant on the database against which you are comparing. So you -- essentially the technicians and the statisticians are at the mercy of the database which they are trying to match. The notion of uniqueness can in fact be manipulated simply by the size of the database. So if what they have for the sake of argument is 8.000 individuals represented by family members who have contributed DNA, then all they can compare it to is those 8.000. Even within the context of this list, it shows that even using that small subset as your database or as your standard, any particular DNA profile can in fact match multiple people. If you increased the sample size of your reference, if you took it from those 8.000 family members to 20.000 family members, it doesn't mean that you are inherently going to get more identifications. It potentially represents that what you will get is people who otherwise would have only matched one individual or -- sorry, DNA profiles that only would have matched one individual could potentially begin to match more. It's not a unique process. The DNA, the 15 alleles that they are looking at, should not be mistaken as equivalent to a fingerprint, and they are not unique to every individual. All of these identifications are based solely on a statement of statistical probability that says, what is the likelihood that those 15 codes match the codes of the 8.000 or 7.000 family members represented in the database? That's all it is. It is not an identification, and even those papers that we reference, those of us who have worked for ICMP and continue to work for ICMP have always recognised that to be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Komar. Now, if I can just for the moment, and I know we were discussing Dean Manning, direct your attention at the SOP from ICMP, specifically P3191. And as you are looking at that and as that's being brought up through e-court for all of us to examine, I note that -- and we used -- or you've used the word "DNAView." Can you just tell me what that means when you say -- what is a DNAView? Is that a machine or a mechanism in which the analysis is being performed?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the computer programme used to calculate and match -- let me rephrase that. Once a DNA profile has been established, it is the computer programme that matches that profile against the database of the family members who have offered their DNA to attempt to make putative matches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have before us the exhibit P3191, and just briefly -- and I -- we see the date, obviously. It's rather conspicuous, the 15th of October, 2002, on the right-hand corner. Now, can you just tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This SOP?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a statement -- an SOP is a standard operating procedure, so ICMP has essentially said that for this step of the DNA identification process, here is the protocol we are going to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All it is is essentially an argument or their justification for the use of DNAView, which is a statistical programme, that calculates the probability that that DNA profile matches other individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you've highlighted, and we'd like to look at the ERN number on this page, which of this document is page 5 of 11, but ERN number is R0637646. And if you can help us with that, it's a discussion under a highlighted caption of "Prior Probability." And help us understand this if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to generate the statistical statement of probability to any one individual identification, the person running the analysis has to set a series of parameters for the computer to follow. So essentially, in some respect you have to tell it what it is you want to do and how you want to calculate it. Prior probability is a statement of what are the chances that one individual belongs to a specific defined population. It's not a statement of who they might be in entirety. It is a statement that says, if I have these 8.000 people what is the probability that this individual is one of those 8.000, not what is the probability of this individual being anyone; simply a statement of the probability of that one individual being part of the subset you have identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you in your analysis and experience both in ICMP and in the scientific community seen that there was a subsequent SOP with respect to this theme by ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a revised protocol. I believe it's either 2006, 2007.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the 3rd of August, 2006, Doctor, and we're going to put it up with, if we may, on the screen. It has the identification or the court number P3224. So if we could take a look at that, and again, I'm going to -- and just because we have the front page, if you could just describe it again, and if you see a date on it just for the record so it isn't that I identified it as being the -- August of 2006. I think you can see it, but I'd like to hear it from you.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please. I believe the date might actually be on the last page. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, I thought it was on the first page as well.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw the upper half of the first page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the bottom right-hand corner. How about if we do this, Doctor. If you don't mind, if I can just -- there it is. It's on the first page. I wasn't sure if they were following -- looking for the last page or the first. Thank you for that, and this is obviously an SOP from ICMP, which is the 6th -- or 3rd of August 2006, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the one you were just referencing?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the second -- that is the revised version of this SOP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If I can direct our attention to page 6 of 16 of this revised SOP, and it bears the ERN number 06248603, and it's under Roman numeral VI in the second paragraph, same caption, "Prior Probability." If you could just enlighten us as to what, if anything, this relates to this paragraph, SOP.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The underlined -- the second underlined sentence highlights that the calculation that is used to establish prior probability has dropped from 8.000 to 7.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So from 2002 through 2006, we see a drop of 1.000, essentially. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They've altered the denominator for prior probability, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what would you do that if you alter that denominator and just place a different number? Would all the numbers ultimately be skewed, like 5.000 or 4.000 or 3.000? What significance, if any, would occur?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, what the prior probability statement does is it gives the computer the basis -- or it gives the programme the basis by which to calculate the probability. When you change the prior probability, you change the outcome. This is a statement reflecting that they no longer believe that 8.000 is the subset of population that they are looking at. They acknowledge that it now stands at 7.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's that denomination or that -- these protocols, I believe, or you could help me with that, that Dr. Parsons in his one-page report utilizes in calculating this statistical or arithmetic equation or percentages, does he not?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't argue that it's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, help us understand it. If it's not, it's not.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, essentially what the number stands for is the -- is a belief in a total number of population that might be represented by victim number or MNI. So it's the number of missing people. Whether you believe that to be 8.000, whether it you believe it to be 7.000 is -- it is essentially what you are telling the computer to use as your basis. The question -- there is a shift within ICMP that occurs approximately about 2006 that the number of 8.000 may not be representative of the total number of victims, and so they have altered how they are calculating the statistical probability for matches down to 7.000. So essentially, it's an argument -- it represents an argument from ICMP that they believe the total number of victims relating to Srebrenica will be 7.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we examine as we did in part yesterday Parsons' report, which is P3005, and we'll wait for that to come up to the screen, what's the relevance of Dr. Parsons utilizing the 8.000 number given the amendment and revision from the 2002 to the 2006 SOP at ICMP?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you don't mind, we'll wait until we get that on the screen so we can see. Oh, that's also under seal. Sorry, thank you. And we have it now. Thank you, Doctor. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: How you set the denominator for your prior probability will determine ultimately the statistical result you receive for your identification. In 2002 by setting it at 8.000, ICMP makes the statement that they believe there will be 8.000 individuals missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's an assumption? Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an assumption based on -- that you would have to make in order to establish that as your parameter. That number isn't given to them by the computer. That number has to be given by the analyst doing the analysis of the DNA in order to make the calculation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dr. Komar, forgive me, but just so the record's clear, that's not an assumption that you're making. That's an assumption that ICMP is making, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That represents ICMP's best determination of what the total number of victims will be in order to get statistically meaningful results from the calculation. In 2006, ICMP modifies that number to 7.000. They feel that it's -- there's sufficient proof that the number will actually be closer to 7.000, and so they begin to do statistical calculations of identity using that number; completely appropriate, it's not uncommon to revise. It would -- the question whether they went back to the identifications that were done in between and recalculated, I can't speak to. That would be best practice. Whether they did it, I don't know. In 2007, Parsons issues a statement that once again suggests he wants to put the number back to 8.100, to be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you find in the evidence or materials that you reviewed any justification for Parsons amending it to 8.100?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: A, there is no suggestion that he's amending anything in the letter because the letter, one, speaks for itself; secondly, the question calls for speculation as to what -- this witness to speculate what is in Dr. Parsons' mind and his motivation for writing the letter, which cannot be gleaned from the face of the letter and, rather, should have been appropriately put to Dr. Parsons. I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my learned friend misunderstood my question. I wasn't asking her to speculate. I asked if there was any evidence that she's seen from reviewing it as to having a basis for Dr. Parsons increasing it. I's not asking her to speculate, and I hope that's clear, but there is in this material, obviously, a change from their very own protocol, and I'm simply asking her if she's found that in the documents that were provided by the OTP for her review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document in question reads in relevant part that "ICMP does not represent that they are strictly true or that the degree of uncertainty can be empirically estimated with accuracy," and that's with respect to the number of 8.100. I think that amply speaks for itself, and to put at that to the witness to interpret what that means I think is completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is that it's a perfectly legitimate question, provided the witness has understood that there is no room for speculation evidence. She can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Komar, we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the risk of inciting a riot, can it be restated to me, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try to find it and restate it so that I don't draw another objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reading it from the transcript isn't going to help you much. You need to remember what you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do. I just didn't want to misstate it, and I would state it verbatim just so I don't draw an objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, did you find in the evidence, in the materials that you reviewed, any evidence to support Dr. Parsons in amending or revising the number up to 8.100 as he does in his 2007, November 30th, letter?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Where?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where we had this conversation or began a conversation yesterday about the difference between matching rate, representation, and collection rate. The argument he puts forth and the Prosecution is absolutely right that is he very cautious in his language in stating that, you know, they are not trying to come up with a number. The reason this is relevant is the 8.100 would go to how they are calculating their probability. He makes the argument that because there is a matching rate of 95.7 plus or minus .54 percent, that there would be a collection -- that - I'll read the language - "and that the total number of missing can" -- I'm sorry. Let me go up. It's hard to read this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we amplify it, please, or can we just blow it up? Thank you. Thank you very much. Okay. In the third paragraph, "Then a simple extrapolation would suggest we have collected reference samples from 95.7 percent of the missing. That's not a fair assumption." He is equating matching rate to collection rate, and that's not -- I would suggest, in my opinion, that's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us why it's not appropriate in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Matching rate goes to a statement of -- a statement of observation, frankly, that says if we have 100 red balloons in one sample and 97 red balloons in another, we have a matching rate of 97 percent. There is a concurrence between the two samples of 97 percent. That's matching rate. Collection rate is a different statement. If you have a population, however you define your population - so for the sake of this particular proceeding, let's say it's the purported victims of Srebrenica - matching rate has nothing to do with collection rate. Collection rate is a statement of how many of the family members relating to potential victims of Srebrenica you have collected data from, and that isn't 95.7 percent. 95.7 percent is a statement of how many bone samples you have matched the database as you've established it to that time from the family members, so it's not a statement of collection rate. Collection rate is how many of the family members have you sampled from, not how many matches have subsequently been made from the DNA profiles extracted from the bones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it fair, and help me understand this, Dr. Parsons' method of doing this, is it -- and I don't want to use the word "flawed" because I don't know Dr. Parsons that well, but is it misleading in any way or is it problematic? I know you said it's inappropriate, but I still don't have an appreciation as to the significance of that inappropriateness.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is very clear, and he uses the word "assumption" multiple times. So he is very clear that he is making an assumptive argument. He's not -- he's not arguing a fact. He is saying that, you know, how do we come up with this lower half of the number to make this prior probability? He makes the argument that if they are getting a matching rate of 95.7 percent when you take the bones and you compare them to the family, he argues that he is making the assumption that, therefore, they're getting a collection rate of 95.7 percent. In my opinion, that's a false assumption and an assumption that would invalidate the conclusion. Ask two experts; get two opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, is there -- in your review of these materials including the 2002 and 2006 SOP by the ICMP and this letter from Dr. Parsons, did you find any other areas of concern or problematic areas that you'd like to share your opinion on?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: State that again. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. We're examining Dr. Parsons' 30th November 2007 letter, and I'm trying to draw from you if you have any other opinions other than those which you've shared with us in connection with the number of 8.100 and the matching and representation issues that you've discussed. Is there anything else that you see with the statistical calculations that in your opinion may be problematic?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm going to direct your attention to your report, which is in the first section where you discuss it. I'd like to ask you before that, what happens to ICMP's matches if 7.000 is incorrect, if the number 7.000 is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a matter of the number 7.000 being incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By changing the denominator, by changing your fundamental prior probability, you change the end result, the statistical assessment of what the possibility may be because they have set a line. There's threshold that each identification must meet. There has to be a -- the number has to be bigger than 99.8 in some cases, 99.5 in others. By changing that statement of prior probability, you change the outcome; you change the statistical outcome. And so that denominator is quite important. It literally determines who gets called a positive identification and who doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, having worked with ICMP and based on your experience, we've seen the protocols, the SOPs, from 2002 and from 2006. Have we seen any -- or have you been able to review any since 2006 which alters or changes that prior probability that we were discussing in these instances?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a moment to review the list? Off the top of my head, I honestly don't remember. If there is a protocol beyond the second protocol for the calculation, I don't know it, if there is one that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think it exists, but I just wanted to be sure, and maybe you've done a more thorough job, and I'm sure you have, of reviewing it. So you have not been able to either review it or you have not been given that document to review, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there is a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, over all, if we look at Dean Manning's conclusions and ICMP's conclusions, do you have an opinion based upon a reasonable degree of certainty as to whether there is a necessity for peer review within the system?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- first, tell me what it is, peer review.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Peer review?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we are familiar with it, but just so we could have a clear understanding.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The foundation of forensic science, academia science, is that work that is produced is reviewed by what are considered your peers or your colleagues. No paper can be printed in a journal that hasn't gone through peer review, no grant application is awarded money absent peer review, and one of the better outcomes of the learning process we went -- that we as a forensic community went through in dealing with these large-scale, large-death investigations is the need for peer review within the process. And that brings up the -- sort of the duelling or conflicting issues of transparency and -- transparency and confidentiality, that essentially you're dealing with restricted material. You're dealing with material that needs to be kept secret or not released from the public versus transparency, which argues that those in the communities and those who -- with a related interest should be able to evaluate how you do things in order to be comfortable with the fact that the process itself is correct. So peer review serves a purpose so that others the community are looking at what you are doing, looking at the reports you write, looking at the conclusions you come to, and saying that there's a collective agreement that the work and the methodology and the analysis and the conclusions are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you cite us an example that may come to mind?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having gone through this process in Bosnia from 1999, 2000, 2001, when we set up the protocols for Iraq, we included peer review of the autopsy reports, the conclusions, and so on. I can also say that JPAC, the US military large-scale identification process, insists on including peer review of its reports and its identifications and its analysis as part of their protocols as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the World Trade Centre? Would that also serve as an example?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They go through peer review in a different manner, but they are certainly a very -- the identification process there can very much be described as a transparent situation. The community at large is very aware of how that is playing out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you, Doctor, involved in at all in any capacity with the 9-11?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at -- yeah, I went to the World Trade Centre within 38 hours of the occurrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just tell us briefly, what was your role while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I volunteered to be part of the recovery effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to your report, specifically Section 1.1, where -- and I was trying to draw this from you, and I apologize for not being able to. In the middle portion of that, you continue in discussing Dr. Parsons' assumptions and analysis. You go on to say that the number of DNA profiles in (5280), then you go on to make the calculation. Can you explain that portion to us again, and what's the significance of it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's essentially the difference between matching rate and collection rate. So he argues that the matching rate should serve as the assumption for how he calculates what the total potential missing would be. I -- this essentially presents how I would argue or make that calculation. So rather than using matching rate, we have to look at -- sorry, if I can pull this in front of me. I'm arguing or suggesting that the -- another way of calculating this would be the number of DNA profiles out of the total reported people. So rather than saying we've managed to match 95.7 percent of the bones to the purported sample, I would argue we should look at how we are looking at our ultimate big number as the percentage of DNA profiles from the total number of reported people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the approach that you are suggesting, and it's a little -- is that a reasonable approach?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's how -- if you invoke the World Trade Centre as an example, that's how that calculation is being done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so it's obviously used elsewhere, so it's accepted in the scientific world, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a precedent for doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. And when calculating it the way you calculated it, you come up with a percent of approximately 68 percent, correct, or 67.9 percent, to be fair, I guess.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's statement of the number of profiles as of this letter versus the number of individuals reported missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you go on to list that -- with the assumptions that were made, you list out five, I think, or four reasons for having this equal chance. Can you just explain that so we can understand that a little better and the significance of it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: His second assumption presented in the letter is, and I'll quote, "That the reason for failing to make a DNA match on a given bone profile is that there is no reference sample present in the database." So it's an argument that says, if we -- if ICMP is not able to make a match, it isn't that the DNA can't be extracted from a bone, it isn't that the individual isn't represented in what's being exhumed, or a variety of other variables. He makes the assumption that the only reason the match would fail to occur is because a family member hasn't given a DNA sample, and I simply wish to highlight the other very reasonable assumptions that should be listed there, that there are other very viable reasons why that match would not occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you proceed in your report to give us in the last sentence there, that -- as you can see it, "Finally, the assumption that there is no existing reference profile presupposes that every single sample produce a viable DNA" - I'm just trying to slow down, Doctor, because they've been very patient with, I think, me at the very least - "which is extremely unlikely given conditions of the remains and other factors impacting DNA preservation." Help me understand that, although I've read it a couple of times and we have discussed it. What are you saying there?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can, again, invoke the World Trade Centre as an example, there are believed to be just less than 3.000 people reported missing, so very much like circumstances like we have here. We have the number of people reported missing. Of that number, only 57 percent have actually been identified and accounted for, so just over 1.500. The same sort of example happens here. You only have a portion identified of what is believed to be the ultimate number, and for me I would be more comfortable using the 7.772 that have been reported missing much as was done in World Trade. So you have family members who have stepped forward and said, we can account for 7.772 people that are reported missing. To assume that you're going to get an identification rate of 95.7 at least of those individuals is not necessarily a realistic assumption because it presupposes that your -- the materials that you are examining are so pristine and producing DNA at a level that has simply never been experienced in any other similar circumstance. It is more realistic to simply look at the results you are getting and accept here are the ones we actually can identify, whatever that number is. There essentially would be two numbers: One is the number of people reported missing by their families; the other would ultimately be the number identified. It's not a moral distinction; it's not a judgement call; it's not a failing of ICMP or any forensic community if the two numbers can't match each other. An identification rate in these circumstances of 100 percent or even 90 percent is not realistic. It's not -- it's not expected, and to try and set an unrealistic goal for oneself isn't necessarily productive in this environment. We should simply be going through the process, identify -- finding as many as possible, identifying as many as possible, and then whatever that number of identifications are, accept it as what it is rather than try and reach a goal of getting every missing person. That hasn't happened in other circumstances, and it's not a realistic goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. In the couple minutes that we have left before our break, I believe, I wanted to go back to this peer review issue that we discussed. From your review of the records, have you seen that there's been any of this peer review in connection with Manning and Parsons and their overall conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many of the ICMP SOPs, there are multiple signatures, which is appropriate, and that's the way an SOP should be written. For all of the reports that I've read, I can see no indication -- essentially when peer review occurs, those who are reviewing it add their signature, not in any way suggesting authorship or otherwise, but there is a record of those who peer review. It's a way of controlling the information, if nothing else. I see no indication that that's occurred. Now, I can't speak to whether every single one of these is an original document that would contain those signatures. There's no reference in the SOPs for sending anything out for peer review, which there should be if it's a standard practice. There should be noted in the SOPs. So based on what has been made available to me, I can see no indication that that has occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thank you. Let me go to another topic, which is a prelude, I think, to my final area that I'd like to discuss with you after the break, and that is, are you familiar with the term "fact shopping"?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me what it means, if you know.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What fact shopping is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a euphemism employed in the scientific community, the forensic community, for only focusing on those features that support your argument and discarding or disregarding those that do not support your argument.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Doctor, having been in the field in Srebrenica and also knowing and I'm sure speaking with your colleagues who have also been involved in the exhumations, did you formulate an opinion as to whether or not the OTP at any time was directing or being involved in the exhumation process? And what I'm getting at is this, and to be honest and fair to my learned friends, was it allowed that the anthropologists and the scientists would be able to look at the evidence and then reach their own conclusion, or was it more conclusion-driven?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object on the ground that it's leading; and secondly, I object also on the basis that it's unclear. It is also vague with respect to whom my learned colleague is referring to when he talks about what's allowed and what's not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doctor, have you understood Mr. Ostojic's question, or do you wish him to clarify it better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would ask that it be restated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Dr. Komar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then he will clarify it. In principle, we agree that it's put and that it could be answered. The witness is perfectly capable of answering that question, and then you can deal with the rest on cross-examination if you so wish. Yes, Mr. Ostojic, if you could rephrase your question in an intelligible way. I'm not saying it wasn't before, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, of course. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I will try to restate the question. Doctor, have you seen through your experience in discussions with colleagues or in articles that were published in connection with the Srebrenica exhumations whether or not the scientists were driven to look at end results as opposed to allowing the evidence to lead them to that end result?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, I object. This is an area that this witness has not spoken about. It's not the subject of the 65 ter summary, it's not the be subject of her report, and we've received no notice with respect to this area of examination from my learned colleague Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll have to look at that, but this witness is a fact witness. I mean, she is a doctor who was at the scene, and she can provide her impressions and opinion in connection with that if she has one, and I'm not sure why it's so difficult for them to understand the question, and it's basically -- she used the euphemism in the scientific world this they use fact shopping. It's very analogous in my view at the very least that it's the end justifying the means, so I think it's appropriate for me to ask her that.
