utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would ask when I used that term in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, actually, it was Mr. Ostojic who used it, not you, but he did ask you whether you understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor, as you see we have been discussing. One conclusion we definitely come to is that the question and the subject matter of the question itself clearly fall outside the area of expertise that -- your expertise, which is what you came here for actually. To give us your expert advice. Assuming that you would agree with us, that this is so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be perfectly comfortable not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely what we were going to asking you. So you move to your next question, please. But we will have the break now. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Nothing to add, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic, how much longer do you have because you have already taken 3 hours and 15, almost 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have approximately 15 to 30 minutes. It's just one last topic that I'd like to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please start to wind it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning still, Doctor, and thank you. I'm going to turn to another topic if I may with you and that's a topic classified as social group identity. Are you familiar with that general categorization?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And describe to us what that is.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If personal identification is putting a name back to a decedent, social group identity is the use of class characteristics to define a population. From an anthropological standpoint that could be a culture group, a national group, a religious group; it is how people are united as a community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your review and analysis of the materials as well as your experience and involvement in some of this, have you been able to examine that material and evidence in connection with social group identity?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have identified the few times it appears in the reports that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your report I think it's reflected in section 5, just so that everyone can follow along with us. And what you've done is look at that topic and then looked at the evidence or the scientific or the investigative evidence from Manning to view how they have applied it in formulating some of your opinions, I believe. So let's look first at Dr. Wright's report of the 12th of May, 1999, which is again -- and we looked at it yesterday, P666. And given the time interests, if I can just direct your attention quickly to page 00848216, which is again the summary of findings. I think there's reference there to Muslim affinity. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you share with us, what is the significance of social group identity?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specific to the charge of genocide it contains, to my understanding which is, you know, perhaps better than a laypersons but certainly not from a legal perspective, it seems that the definition includes this notion of social group identity, that the victims must constitute a group and it must be one of the protected groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen through this material that you reviewed whether or not that issue was analysed and reviewed in connection with the exhumations that were conducted?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several comments to the effect of the affinity of the victims, that's all I've seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the next page of Dr. Wright's report which is 00848217, I think that's where Dr. Wright discusses that they are not going to study the bodies in the associated artifacts, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a statement that said it is not the primary purpose of the exhumation programme to study the bodies and the associated evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do they proceed to do that, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some degree. In isolated instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in analyzing Baraybar's report of the 8th of December, 1999, and I apologise that we are moving a little fast, which is identified as P560, again specifically directing your attention to page number 00911867, does he summarize, if at all, as to what should be done in connection with this social group identity?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can answer as I understand, essentially, he takes a different approach, a more cautious approach, in my mind a more appropriate approach. He notes the presence of what he defines as religious artifacts but he doesn't ascribe a particular religious affinity to what is found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he takes a different approach from whom?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Richard Wright's prior approach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is that, to the extent you would know scientifically speaking, of course. I'm not asking you to speculate as to why Baraybar has taken a different approach but is there any significance as to Baraybar taking a different approach from Dr. Wright's approach?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the significance of that, if any?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mr. Baraybar does is essentially he simply describes what is being found. They both follow the same essential SOP or protocol in the field in that they both recognise that given the circumstance, the time constraint and the need to examine the material in more detail, it's appropriate not to be making determinations or assessments in the field. So what Mr. Baraybar does in his report is simply note the presence of objects without defining what it is he interprets them to mean. What Mr. Wright does in his report is he ascribes a meaning, he interprets what he sees and ascribes a meaning to it, he assigns them a category.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found through the evidence that you reviewed that actually there was an effort to identify the social group?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you rephrase that, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure, I'll try. From your review of the documents and materials in connection with examining and providing evidence in this case, have you found that the scientific evidence supports that they have found concretely a social group identity for the bodies that were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is that there hasn't been sufficient work on this area to make any kind of definitive conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at Manning's witness statement, Mr. Manning's witness statement of the 24th of October, 2003, and just so the record's clear and we can follow it, yesterday I think we identified it as 1D357, however, the correct number in e-court is P551. I just wanted to carry it so that when we review it later we would be able to follow it. Thank you for that. So it's P551. And specifically I'll direct your attention to X -- page X0169261.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is incorrect, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite get that. Which number is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would we be able to get some assistance as to what the correct number is? It's specifically previously identified as 1D357. Again just so that we are clear which document it is, it's a witness statement of Dean Manning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand it's P3551.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 24th November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of 2003. Thank you. 24th of November, 2003. Again it's P3551. And Dr. Komar, quickly I'd like to direct your attention to page 23 of his report, which has the ERN number X0169261, and specifically paragraphs 83, which is simply a caption, and then 84 is what I'd like to ask you about. Have you been able to review this document in connection with your review of the materials in this case?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the significance, if any, that you may have with respect to paragraph number 84, and the section obviously captioned "Evidence of Muslim religious affiliation"?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a very brief summary of the source of -- or what he cites as his source for making a determination of evidence of Muslim affiliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion based upon a reasonable degree of certainty if that was thorough or is it acceptable to merely make this conclusion based on some of the material that he cites, given the scientific evidence that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is a completely speculative question. There's no indication that this is represented to be exclusive information that Mr. Manning relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you wish to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I could walk through it, I don't agree with my learned friend but I'll walk, if I may, through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then do that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned friend suggests that this isn't the exclusive evidence that Mr. Manning relied upon. Have you, Doctor, been able in the course of your review of the materials in this case been able to find any other sources identified by Dean Manning to support anything other than that which he is saying in the limited fashion that he does in this report?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment to what he has reviewed. Of the material I've reviewed, the sections that have been pointed out in the Wright report and in the Baraybar report and similar statements in their subsequent reports with no more detail represents what I have found from the scientific reports that expressly directly address this area. I have no knowledge of what Mr. Manning had or reviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he in any of his reports or his statements or testimony, does he give a basis as to what it is that he reviewed or can reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go through and review everything that he submitted. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, does Mr. Manning, with respect to the evidence of Muslim religious affiliation, follow the methodology that was outlined by Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The methodology?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way in which or the example and how Dr. Baraybar summarizes this social group identity, that -- does Manning, is he consistent with that or inconsistent, in the approach that Manning has -- that Baraybar has suggested as we saw on P560 just recently?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Baraybar suggests a methodology. He adopts an appropriate and conservative approach to simply describing what he sees rather than attempting to analyse what he sees. The statement that's before me here appears to be a conclusion of an analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion with respect to this conclusion of an analysis by Dean Manning as to the appropriateness of it or not?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the significance of the question of religious affiliation to the issues, specifically of genocide, overall what I see I don't feel there's compelling evidence that this question has been adequately addressed from a scientific perspective. Again, because the references to it are so brief and so cursory, it feels to me as though this particular topic given the weight it carries has not received sufficient scientific scrutiny given that there are methods of determining religious affiliation even in a decedent group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are some of those methods, if you can enlighten us?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different methods. Essentially what you are looking for are the class characteristics that define how you are defining your population. So say for the purposes of this examination, we are looking at the idea of who gets called a Muslim. A Muslim is a religious affiliation; it's adherence to the Islamic faith. There are several methods that one can go about defining that or recognizing whether or not someone would be included in that particular population that include to some extent what is vaguely alluded to here what would be called the analysis of material culture. So material culture are those artifacts and items that are associated with an individual, the clothing you wear, the materials you carry, the jewellery, your documents and so on. So a proper and complete analysis of material culture would be one means of establishing that -- a religious affiliation. A second means would be through the positive identification of individuals provided there were sufficient anti-mortem social data available that what then allow to track those individuals back and see if, in fact, there is any social data, membership within a mosque, even family reported data to support what religious affiliation those individuals might have claimed in life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are reasonable approaches or reasonable methodologies that could and should be utilized in determining social group identity?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have been adopted elsewhere, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this case, Doctor, or in the materials that you reviewed, have you found that they as you said, I think in the Wright report that they mention it but in a cursory fashion and they basically don't follow up and apply this approach or methodology that's widely accepted or accepted elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the materials I've reviewed essentially what there is is two statements from the field, one by Mr. Baraybar that is cautious and simply describes what he has been found; the other is by Richard Wright who makes an assessment, who actually categorizes the victims based on what he has seen. Both of those individuals are following a protocol that says analysis is not being conducted in the field particularly of the material culture. So one would have to few those statement as cursory and preliminary at best and not based on a full assessment of the material. If there is any subsequent report generated at autopsy or in any other form that expressly looks at the material culture and evaluates in terms of the question of religious affiliation, I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your answer just now following a protocol that says analysis is not being conducted in the field particularly of the material culture, what protocol are you referring to? First, who set the protocol to the extent you know and where can we find it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It occurs first in Richard Wright's first report, his first field exhumation report which talks about the standard operating procedure and mentions on several occasions that analysis cannot and would not be done in the field because the clothes are dirty, they are not going through the pockets, they prefer - and it's completely appropriate - that subsequent analysis occur at autopsy in the lab later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to know whether or not my colleague Mr. Ostojic is actually contesting the question of the victim group affiliation in this case because otherwise, I don't see that this is a relevant line of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just briefly to address that. The Defence does not carry the burden of proof on any one element. This is a specific element that the Prosecution carries the burden of proof on at all times. To ask me that question would be unfair, and it would permit me to testify which I, if the counsel wants, would be willing to on a number of different topics, but I suggest that it wouldn't be prudent. I think they care carry the burden of proof, and they should ask this question to themselves and not direct it towards me, respectfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the time being, and we reserve our position on this for later depending on what we get in return, we are going to ask the witness, the expert witness to answer the question if you can and if you wish to, and then we take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can the question be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to do it, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. We weren't addressing you. We were addressing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. If you wish to repeat the question, yes, of course, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you were starting to answer. That specific element as we've identified it, and I'm sure during cross, if they have it, they'll produce it. With respect to social group identity, have you found evidence to support that that's been scientifically and reasonably identified and conducted?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I've reviewed, I don't feel that the issue has received sufficient attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the extent -- other than the extent that we've discussed here, and that would be Wright's report of the 12th of May, 1999, where he sets out the protocol and what not to do as you've suggested and Baraybar's report of the 8th of December, 1999, and given Manning's statement that we've just looked at, the 24th of November, 2003, specifically Exhibit P3551, any other evidence that that's not only been significantly established but established at all?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of no other source. Based on the protocol that's established in the field, it would suggest that any subsequent analysis would have been done at autopsy and that, therefore, any additional comments would come from that source. If anything other than that was done, I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And certainly, Dr. Komar, having met you recently and engaging with you here this last day and so, if they had that material you'd be happy to look for it and you'd be happy to give an opinion in connection with that. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- I think we can move to your next question. Don't answer that question, Madam, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, with respect to some of the exhumations that you've done - and I'm almost nearing the end and trying to be as fair as possible with you - so I showed you a document which is on our exhibit list, which has previously been identified as 1D374. It's a document from the United Nations dated the 17th of July, 1995. And just so the Court understands and my learned friend, I'm not going back to this issue of fact shopping and the ends justifying the means, but I'd like to just have you look at the second page of that document, if you will, and again, it's 1D374. We are just waiting for it to come up on the screen. Doctor, I think you may have seen this document before starting your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the first page of it? Is it possible? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You presented this to me a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just if we can -- I can direct your attention to the second page of that document. The first full paragraph immediately before the second paragraph number 2, there's a small indentation that I'd like to focus our attention on. But before I put the question to you, I'll allow my learned friend to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is -- goes back to the same objection I made previously. This is not the subject of this witness's expert report. It has not been previously referred to, and we've been on -- not put on any notice of this issue, and I think this is a fundamental problem with respect to this issue. We additionally weren't provided with a proofing note with respect to this matter, even though the witness apparently has been presented with it and has had an opportunity to evaluate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's certainly on our exhibit list that we've tendered to my learned friend. I don't need the document, perhaps, to ask this question, but I'm going allow the Court to rule on it. I disagree with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That make it worse because if you eliminate the document, then Mr. Vanderpuye's argument becomes stronger in the sense that you did not give an indication of this in the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We gave -- obviously, we gave the report of Dr. Komar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to your next area because it is definitely not in the area of expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Doctor in conducting the exhumations that you've conducted, were you able to notice when you actually physically do that exhumation as to whether or not some bodies sustained any shrapnel wounds?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't do that analysis in the field. I would do that analysis in autopsy. I have in autopsy in -- just to answer a question in a general form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you done it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have I done it at autopsy?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Have you done it in connection with the fieldwork that you'd done -- that you'd performed in the Srebrenica graves that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structure of how these exhumations and autopsies work are such that when you are doing the field season you do your field season, and then the material is leased to a morgue. The times I've spent in the morgue were not directly associated with the material that I did in the field, so I can't speak to -- specifically to Srebrenica because while I may have conducted field exhumations in Srebrenica, I cannot be sure that I then examined those bodies at autopsy. I've worked at the PIP morgue, which is associated with Srebrenica remains, but I cannot be positive that any one particular set of remains is associated with the specific events of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also -- just in this area, and this is nearing the end here. With respect to the social group identity, you've identified in some -- in your report the bibliographies which establish such identities. I just want to get this document in. I think it's 2D544, and if you can just confirm to us or inform us of what this document is. It's, again, 2D544.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my arrival here, I was asked if the question of social group identity has not been adequately addressed, what methods have been adopted in the past and what are the protocols and standards that have been set. This is by no means an exhaustive bibliography. It is simply a -- what -- some of the references I had available at my disposal in terms of how we go about addressing, how we would establish independently and scientifically what the social group identity of a collection of individuals would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may just try to put it in a little more legalese, if you -- I think you'll understand me, and it's scientific as well. If this bibliography highlights for us acceptable methods in which to determine the social group identity, it's not an exhaustive list, we understand, but it provides that methodology that you find in a scientific world as being acceptable, correct?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It represents how this has been established in the past. This question of acceptability is a Court question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Dr. Komar, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours, for your patience. I just have to say one thing if I'm allowed. It's really more on a personal matter, so I don't know if I should say it in public or in private, but I've been -- I have a personal crisis that I have to tend to, so I just want to apologise to the Court. I'm going to leaving at 12.30 to go back to Chicago, and I want to I apologise to Dr. Komar and just so the Court knows as to why I won't be here later this afternoon. And my colleague Mr. Nikolic is more than capable to address any issues that may arise during cross-examination. Thank you, Dr. Komar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That puts Mr. Nikolic on stand by. He will need to be present all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I should be back on Monday. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, you'll -- okay. That makes it easier. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Now, Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Likewise, Mr. President, no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nor do we Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, good morning, Dr. Komar. I'd like to start off really where Mr. Ostojic left off by thanking you for your evidence, it's been interesting, informative and very succinct, if I may say so. But I'd just like to pick up on two or three points relating to some of the matters you've covered with Mr. Ostojic. And the first is really the question of the calculation of the MNI. Now, you told us yesterday that you first observed the use of that term in the various reports you've read in the report of Mr. Wright composed, I think, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the date, it's whatever the first Wright report is when I have seen the first statement of a scientific calculation MNI, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. And then you went on to explain in some detail the rather different method of calculation employed by Mr. Baraybar. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like, as it were, to throw into the melting pot a third variant and to do that I would ask, please, that P00622 be placed into e-court and the witness will need to see pages 75 to 76, and those who speak Serbian will need to see pages 76 to 77. Just so there's no mystery about this, Dr. Komar, this is the report of Dr. Hagland which I think you have considered.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I've read the specific report. I've certainly read many of Mr. Hagland's reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. Do you now have in front of you, Dr. Komar, a page which should have in its top right-hand corner the number 62?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is it sufficiently blown-up for to you read it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this version, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you just take the trouble to read the paragraphs under the heading "Determination of Minimum Number of Individuals and Missing Body Parts." And when you've got to the bottom of the page, ask the usher to flick it over and you can have a look at the next bit.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Is it possible to scroll down past the -- thank you. Keep going, please. Does it extend beyond the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could keep going, please. Do I need to extend beyond "Summary of plausible scenarios"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Dr. Komar. I'll put the question to you and if you need to read any more then we'll give you that opportunity. Firstly, I ought to just check, had you seen that document or that part of that document before?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you aware that prior to, as it were, Mr. Baraybar overseeing the exhumations in relation to the Srebrenica investigation, Mr. Hagland had overseen a series of exhumations himself?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. The substance of the question I want to put to you is this: That is a method of calculating MNI, isn't it, that Mr. Hagland there describes?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But it is a rather different method from that employed by Mr. Baraybar, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So when we come to look at, as it were, the calculation of MNI by the Prosecution, we are not just looking at the method employed by Mr. Wright and the method employed by Mr. Baraybar, we are looking at three different methods, that employed by Mr. Wright, that employed by Mr. Hagland and that employed by Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would also suggest that a fourth is introduced with the DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. While we are with that document, I just want to head out into some rather dangerous water and ask that you look at page 82 in the English, and for the Serbian speakers that's page 83. Don't worry about the numbers on your page, the page numbers I'm giving relate to the computerized document. And if you would, I'd just like it if you read to yourself, please, the top paragraph headed "Acknowledgments."

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in particular, the penultimate sentence which reads: "Finalisation of cause and manner of death as well as editing of autopsy reports occurred under the direction of ICTY legal advisor Peter McCloskey." You've been asked about, as it were, fact shopping and the drivers behind the work on the ground, in your experience on the ground, was that level of prosecutorial involvement common?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to the question. I think there's nothing in the document that even suggests what level my colleague is referring to and if he could specifically make that clear, I would have no objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Haynes, can you restrict your question to the exact wording of the paragraph or that part of the paragraph that you read, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In your experience, were reports finalized under the direction of ICTY Prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports of investigators and ICTY members contributed to final reports, reviewed final reports, I personally have never had a report amended by a legal advisor. I have certainly had them revised by investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would that include, as this document suggests, autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have not had an autopsy report revised by an ICTY member.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's not be naive, you didn't work in a vacuum. Were you ever aware of that being done to any report prepared by any of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I allowed to discuss -- that strikes me as gossip or hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, we don't need gossip. From your personal knowledge, I think. As far as your personal knowledge goes, are you in a position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen it done, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Komar. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Which brings us to you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Komar. My name is a Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution I'll put some questions to you in relation to your direct testimony. I hope it won't be too long but I can't guarantee anything. If I say anything or I ask you question that's not clear to you, just, please, let me know and I'll try to rephrase it in a manner that we can both understand each other. As you've been testifying, you know to try to speak a little slowly so that these matters can be interpreted to all the other members here. Now, you are obviously a very experienced forensic anthropologist; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that I have experience in this area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, the contributions of forensic anthropologists such as yourself to the identification systems with respect to the investigation of mass fatalities are to help locate and recover human remains; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And it's also to examine the biological characteristics that potentially bear on the process of individual identification?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Or personal identification?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you look at things like age at death?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sex?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Stature?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And a host of other osteo-biological information?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And part of your job is to interpret skeletal evidence of trauma?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's also part of your job to identify the presence or absence of trauma?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to differentiate between ante-mortem and postmortem and peri mortem trauma?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the remains that are located, it would also be part of your function to separate or re-individualise remains, reassociate them?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two different ideas, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You would do both?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in general, the contribution of forensic anthropologist through identification process also depends on what the object of that process is; that is, to identify particular individuals in whole or to identify whether or not a particular individual is represented in a given population?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly requested to slow down and to make pauses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I do hear it and I'll try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So there could be a process that's undertaken in order to, for example, return all of the skeletal remains or remains of an individual who is identified in a mass fatality situation or case to a family member?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in that particular circumstance you would evaluate all these osteobiological information in order to establish that when you return those remains, you are not returning somebody else's remains to the wrong family, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be a portion of the process, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's typically involved in a humanitarian effort such as identifying and returning the remains of missing people?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where the object of a given undertaking is to identify whether or not somebody is simply represented in the pool of remains that are located, forensic anthropology also has a contribution to make with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that has to do with basically the same thing, trying to establish, reassociate as many bones as you can under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a portion of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So in a situation, for example, like the World Trade Centre events of September 11th, where you have highly fragmented remains, that would be a situation where it would be possible but perhaps difficult to evaluate certain osteobiographical information in order for the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel and witness are kindly asked to slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- for the purpose of establishing a personal identity with respect to those remains?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the question asked whether the fragmentation confounds that effort, is that a fair --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Makes it more difficult?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you, of course, recognise that DNA testing in general is quite well-established technology?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you recognise, of course, that it's widely used in the context of both criminal and civil proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's used in the systems of identification in the context of mass fatalities?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Such as natural disasters?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Acts of terrorism, conflicts?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's used in that capacity because DNA is unique to a given individual, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of identical twins, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of identical twins.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complete DNA code is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in the case of mass fatalities, DNA analysis can, A, assist in ongoing medical and legal evaluations?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. It can also be used to associate fragmented remains?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it can also actually identify individual victims?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can form the basis of an opinion as to identification, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So for example, where you have a pre-existing sample of a given person's DNA, their own DNA, as it were - toothbrush, comb, something - and a sample is recovered from the site of a mass fatality. You can establish that person's individual identity through matching their respective samples?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are comparing self to self. That is a match. That is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you accept at least in principle that the DNA analysis can establish in the case of mass fatalities that a person is dead and that a person is represented or persons -- part of a person is represented in the remains that are found at a given location?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that a DNA profile consistent with the individual -- again, are we matching self to self or matching to other things?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll do it first self to self.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self to self, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And then with respect to what's called a kinship analysis, that is, comparing blood relatives to the sample in question, do you accept that DNA analysis can establish, A, that the person is at the location where the DNA is ostensibly gathered and that they match that person familially?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm uncomfortable with the term "match." What you're talking about there is a statement of statistical probability that would form the basis of an opinion as to whether that relationship is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in your experience, to the extent that you are familiar with matches in the context of kinship DNA analysis, are you aware of what the statistical thresholds are with respect to declaring a kinship match?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be established by the SOP or protocol for the organisation responsible for conducting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the ICMP in particular, having familiarized yourself with the standard operating procedure, are you aware of what the statistical threshold is with respect to establishing a match?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is contained in their SOP, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that the statistical level of surety with respect to declaring a match that is followed in the ICMP is a threshold level of 99.95 percent?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For non-tentative matches, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware that it is 99.0 percent with respect to presumptive -- where there is, I should say, presumptive evidence of a match?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you spoke earlier on your direct testimony about the significance of what are called prior odds or prior probability?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms -- okay. And that is a number that is used to calculate the end reliability of a putative match?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could have in 65 -- could I have 65 ter 3479, please, in e-court. I should say that this is -- it's under seal, so we should avoid broadcasting it. What I'd like to show you, what is depicted here in e-court, is an example of a match report that is issued by the ICMP, and I just want to focus your attention, if I could, first in the area where you see it says "donors," and what it indicates there are who the donors are: wife, son, daughter, mother. Okay. If we proceed further down the page, you can see where it says "results of matching." Now, with respect to the results of matching, you can see here in this particular example that the DNA results obtained from the bone sample are 29.5e9 times more likely if the bone sample originated from an individual related to the blood references in a manner as described on this report than to another unrelated individual in the general population." It then says, "The probability of relatedness as described on this report is 99.999976 percent when using prior odds of 1/7.000." First, if you could tell us, 29.5e9: What is that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is known as a likelihood ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what does that express in terms of numbers because...

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, it's a statement of likelihood that if this sample were drawn from another source - and we'll define what they mean by "general population," I assume, in a moment - that there is a likelihood that the individual is more closely related to the sample than to the general population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, 25.5e9 stands for what? Is that a million, billion, trillion?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: E to the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an extrapolation of the number, so yes, it's a huge number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's 29.5 trillion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So this report basically reads that the bone sample that was obtained was 29.5 trillion times more likely if it originated from the individual related to the blood references in the manner described in this report, these references, than it would to be another individual in a general population?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As general population is defined by ICMP, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And this would denote an extremely high level of assurance?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A likelihood ratio is not a level of assurance. It's a statement of probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Then it would be an extremely high statement of probability?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the prior odds of 1 in 7.000, how does that influence that number of 29.5 trillion?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't effect that number. It affects the statement of the 99.9999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what if that number were to change to 1 in 6.000? How does that effect 99.9999?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last few digits would shift slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say "last few digits" --

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the comma, 9999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So 76 might change?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Potentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And how does that influence the statement of probability as is indicated in this report?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement of probability? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The 29.5 trillion.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The likelihood ratio?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, the likelihood ratio.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you are asking me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that affect it significantly, in any significant manner or not, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given the size of the number, I would not argue it's a significant change, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what if that -- all right. I'll leave that alone. Well, the probability of relatedness is a different question than the level of surety.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And the threshold for the level of surety in order for the ICMP to issue this report is what?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The threshold of surety?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, of surety?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 99.95 number? I don't know if this is a tentative or putative match or not. It's whatever is in their ICM -- their protocol for --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this was a putative match or not -- or tentative match or presumptive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, assuming that it's -- assuming that it -- there is a -- it is not a presumptive match --

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- the threshold would be -- for the probability of relatedness would be 99.95 percent?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure you're not confusing likelihood statement and probability, so we'll stick to that 99.9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If that's what is in their protocol, then that's their standard, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I may have misunderstood you, but you seem to have indicated that when it comes to the question of unique DNA, that there is a possibility that a unique DNA as designated by ICMP is not unique.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in your estimation, what is that possibility, if you can state it as a ratio?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't attempt to qualify it unless I was sure of what the sample size you were referring to was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you specifically referenced a number of 816 unique DNA profiles.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number was drawn from a database that I was given from the ICMP as of October, I believe it was 8th, 2007, which was their list of what they were calling unique biological.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to their calling these unique biological profiles, am I correct to say that your position is that they don't -- they are not unique?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The possibility exists that they may not be because what determines uniqueness in this particular case is a comparison of that to a defined reference sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So if you have a situation where you have siblings, and you are seeking to establish whether or not those siblings' DNA exist in a given pool, you can do that by conducting a kinship analysis?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you can -- you can establish that each one of those siblings is related to the donor. That is the familial reference sample.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if evidence of both is found.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Only if evidence of both is found?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is, you can establish in the same way that a given individual is related to a given set of parents, for example, family, for either one of those siblings?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking a reverse paternity test?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about making a kinship analysis for Brother A to Parent A and Brother B to Parent A.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can do that?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- with the proper circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in doing so, in making these types of full sibling comparisons, it may be the case that you cannot determine which profile corresponds to which sibling?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Although you can determine that both profiles correspond to Parent A.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are assuming there are two separate profiles?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Assuming that they are two separate profiles.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. In the case where there's one profile, you can establish that the one profile relates to Parent A, right?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be a statement of probability that that relation happens, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, such as a match report?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But it's not possible to know unless you have two profiles whether or not that individual profile corresponds to Brother A or Brother B?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in the presence of two profiles, you would not be able to differentiate them based solely on the DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So it's possible to have a DNA match wherein you do not know within a limited group of individuals to whom the particular profile corresponds?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not use the term "match" in that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But it is possible to have a DNA profile where you know that it is related to a particular family or particular blood donors without knowing whom in a given -- or a limited class of individuals that DNA profile corresponds to?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you rephrase that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll try.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'll use myself as an example. My DNA is recovered from a given location, but my mother reports my brother and I missing. It's possible to know that the DNA profile is one that relates to my mother's children, but it's not possible necessarily to know if it relates to me or my brother. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can technically be true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so in the case where you have an individual DNA profile, that would certainly correspond to an individual, although it's not clear to whom it corresponds?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could correspond to several individuals in your scenario. So if you took the example of you and your brother, just because a DNA sample exists doesn't mean we know the number of people that it potentially could match.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Assuming that the reporting is accurate, that is that there are only two of us that could be in those graves, then in that case you can make that determination?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the reference sample you are comparing that DNA profile to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's make it more specific then. Let's make it that we are talking about a sample that is compared to both parents of the subject.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying. It's not about who you are taking the reference back to. It is the comparison -- not only are you comparing child to family. In order to create these statements that you are referencing here, you then have to go the next step and compare that degree of relationship to an outside source. So if you do it in a small scale, you would compare it to other reference individuals related to Srebrenica. If you do it in a larger scale, what they are calling general population, they are actually comparing it to 423 supposedly or assumed to be unrelated individuals from the Balkans. If you took it to the general population as a whole, if you compared it to the US database of sex offenders and opened it up to a completely unrelated -- or presumed unrelated population, you would end up with a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, is there something that you found that is methodologically improper when comparing a given sample to the general population that's based upon that sample of that population, in terms of DNA analysis, is there something methodologically problematic with that process from that your point of view?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that chunk of it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in fact, that particular process is employed in establishing -- establishing DNA databases and in comparing DNA information across all kinds of populations. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you have a given sample of DNA that is taken in order to establish certain classifications among different groups of people such as people from a particular race, people from a particular region, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That gets into haplogroup analysis, and that's a different aspect of DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you say that they're comparing it against group of 423 group of individuals in terms of establishing what the frequency of a particular characteristic is within that population group, that is how DNA is normally compared, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frequency of an allele to -- within that population, yes, that's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And there's nothing methodologically improper -- there's nothing methodologically --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down both for the record and for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, especially you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's nothing methodologically improper about making that comparison based upon a sample of the population?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand you've said it up to this point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, there is, or yes, there isn't?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there anything wrong -- there is nothing wrong with doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't have the access to the database that you have in front of you, but I'd ask if I could have that up in e-court somehow. Great. Now, you've indicated that you've seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I truly apologise for interrupting, but we did send that to the OTP a couple of days ago, actually, in an attachment, so I think they should have it. We did clearly send that material to them when Dr. Komar was here, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I acknowledge that I have it. I'm not saying that I don't. I just want to refer to it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've indicated that you've found certain instances in which a DNA profile is attributed to more than one person.

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just indicate where you see that on the screen just now?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pointing to -- my cursor to a number of them, so I've essentially grouped them together, and they run on for some time, so this -- all of this section for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I believe the names in this circumstance are -- well, there's confidentiality issue with respect to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think maybe it would be wise to go into private session, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's easily done. Let's go into private session for short while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you want me to start again so that...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There certainly has been, so far as those who defend are concerned, since January the 23rd been a standing request for disclosure of information establishing the identity of exhumed persons, and I do make the observation because I'm specifically asked to that it does, rather, seem to us in any event that under the rules of the Tribunal that material ought to have been disclosed anyway but -- without the need for a request. But there has been a standing request for that since January, which appears to have gone into abeyance for a number of months until there was a meeting at the end of last month and a further series of specific requests by e-mail, which ultimately were refused by the Prosecution on the 5th of July. I'm conscious of the fact that the precise intent behind what was sought is likely to be the subject of debate, but in any event, I do wonder where we are going with this witness being asked about it. Plainly, she would have liked to have seen it. Plainly she hasn't seen it, and I do invite the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber to consider whether this line of prosecution -- this line of cross-examination is fruitful or relevant. And I would invite you to say that it should stop now and that the material which has undoubtedly been requested should be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could briefly speak to the matter of the requests of -- that were related to the Popovic witness that we most -- we may most recall -- we can call it the pherograms issue, and I think -- you clearly recall from Your Honours' question, Mr. President's question, that it -- this -- that Mr. Pherograms - sorry, I can't remember his name - never asked his own counsel for it and counsel never asked us for it. Now, and I believe they did that strategically as they did the same thing with their exhumation expert who wanted more documents but couldn't provide a full opinion because he wasn't provided all the pathological reports, and we were never asked about that, either. We see the same thing happening with pherograms, that I can't give you my opinion because I don't have the reports. Now, factually, since then they have asked us for massive numbers of these things that we considered and we refused because we don't think it's been done in good faith, and it's a massive amount of material. The witness has already testified. We don't want to go back into time. I don't think it was good faith. I think it was a strategy they made, and so that's why we've refused that. That doesn't have anything do with this witness. This witness clearly asked the -- I'll let Mr. Kweku get into this witness, but just to remind you of the situation with the Popovic witnesses, that's where we are there. It's clear to me that we were not asked for anything for this witness. We are checking to see if ICMP was asked. I could also ask the Court whether you were asked to provide a subpoena for such materials. Everyone knows that that is something that's available if that can be said. It's, of course, a critical issue to this expert that she has questions. She's making significant critical comments of her former colleagues in a very important case. She has questions. She needs them answered. I want her to have those -- that material if she -- if it's reasonable. It didn't come to us. We just got word from talking to ICMP's people. They were never asked, as far as they can see from the record. So this goes, of course, to a very important question as you can tell from Mr. Vanderpuye's last question. It was the first time she tended to evade in her answer where she was asked, Well, shouldn't you have reviewed this material before making a critical comment about colleagues, and she was evasive. So this is an important area of cross-examination. I will stop there because it's Mr. Vanderpuye's cross-examination, but to suggest it's not an appropriate area of cross-examination is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, just one question before we can discuss -- just one moment. Have you finished with your line of questions on this issue, or do you have further questions? Especially considering that Mr. Ostojic is no longer with us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry, I haven't had an opportunity to look to see where I wound up before the break. I think I'm practically finished with it, but I'm just not certain because I can't remember now exactly where I left off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. We'll give you time by giving the floor to Ms. Tapuskovic, and in the meantime, please check.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just in order to clarify certain things in this discussion about disclosure on the part of the Prosecution, we can say that the issue of electropherograms was raised only when Mr. Parsons testified. However, it arises from the testimony of Mrs. Komar and Mr. Stojkovic, that the electropherogram is not enough for anybody to establish whether the procedure of identification was carried out correctly. That is why before Parsons', Stojkovic's, and Komar's testimony, we requested from the Prosecution to submit identification records for all the exhumed. The three Defence teams have comprised the entire documentation, whatever you may call it, which concerns the establishment of the identity of all the exhumed persons. Therefore, I believe that the Popovic team and the Nikolic team and the Beara team have in due time, far before the beginning of Defence case and before Mr. Parsons' testimony, has put a very well defined request, and that was on the 23rd of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey. And please, keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As -- Mr. President, no, we've -- this has not been a trial of -- so far where the Defence have been concerned about discovery issues. We have done our best to provide everything, and if there were any issues they would have come back to us. There's never been an issue that she's talking about. I don't know what she is talking about. If they needed more, we got more. The only time we've ever come across a situation where we've said no was with the pherogram issue because we did not -- we thought it was overly burdensome. That train was gone from the station, and I didn't think it was in good faith. This thing she just said is absolutely not founded. If we'd had an issue with them, it would have been raised. Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Zivanovic, they'll take me on when they don't think they are getting something they need, and we know that, but they never took us on on this, and -- so I don't know what they are talking about, and it's frankly probably a side issue at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more sentence, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the testimony of expert Stojkovic on the 30th of June this year, we had a meeting both with the expert Stojkovic, Mrs. [as interpreted] Vanderpuye, and Mrs. Nikola Osevic [phoen], and we considered options as to what should be disclosed to the Defence, and he was requested to specify at that meeting that we held in the afternoon hours what should be disclosed. Mr. McCloskey should be absolutely clear what we are talking about. We had a meeting regarding the additional disclosure after that particular testimony, and that was all confirmed in a subsequent e-mail, and the e-mail provides the list of documents that were requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can clarify that, and I agree with that. That's post the testimony of the pherogram witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just -- the person I've been referring to as Mr. Pherograms is Mr. Stojkovic, just for the record. I apologise for not recalling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, had you exhausted your line of questions on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I've had a chance to review it, and I think -- I don't see any reason to continue in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we can proceed with your next line of questions. Let's get the witness back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd just like to say, we could have achieved all that without troubling you. That's what I asked Mr. Vanderpuye to do at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, but he needed to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Good afternoon, Dr. Komar. I just want to clarify one other thing with you, if I could, with respect to the data that you had on your computer there. In the section of the data where I referred to you -- where I referred you to the protocol ID number, is it right to say that that protocol ID number represents a match made with respect to DNA from a particular individual?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be more accurate to say that it represents a DNA profile extracted from an element, a skeletal element. The use of individual -- unless I'm not understanding you. If you are saying, does a DNA profile equal an individual, I can concede you that, but what we are talking about here is a representation of whatever it was cut from. So I'm not -- if I've answered your question, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think so. Whatever it was cut from comes from one person as opposed to another person; in other words, it's discrete?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you had referred to Dean Manning's reports, I think, in a number of areas on your direct -- in your direct testimony. In particular, you talked about his characterization of certain information as reflecting victim group affiliation or identifying the group as Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's primarily from his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, are you suggesting that the identification of the group that Dean Manning is referring to as being Muslim is based solely upon an examination of -- I believe it was a Koran and some prayer beads?

utterances.speaker: DEBRA KOMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Base on the very short extract that's included, it's actually difficult to tell. He references specific items, and all of the items he references reflect material culture. If there is another source of information at that time, I don't know what it is.
